steps.action: Perform time-out: verify patient identity, procedure, level, laterality, allergies, and anticoagulation status.
steps.safety: Cervical TFESI carries higher risk than lumbar due to proximity to the vertebral artery and spinal cord. Ensure informed consent specifically addresses stroke and spinal cord injury risk.
steps.teaching: The vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen at C6 and ascends through C2. Radiculomedullary arteries supplying the anterior spinal artery may traverse the cervical foramen.

steps.action: Review MRI/CT to confirm target level. Evaluate foraminal anatomy and vertebral artery position.
steps.safety: Identify any anomalous vertebral artery course or foraminal stenosis that may preclude safe needle placement.
steps.teaching: Pre-procedure CT angiography may be considered in high-risk cases. An anteriorly positioned vertebral artery increases procedural risk at that level.

steps.action: Position patient supine with slight neck extension, or lateral decubitus. Place shoulder roll if needed for access.
steps.safety: Supine positioning allows patient to communicate and reduces risk of vasovagal events. Ensure IV access for emergency medication.
steps.teaching: Many practitioners prefer the oblique/lateral approach with the patient supine for cervical TFESI. This provides an anterior-to-posterior trajectory toward the posterior foramen.

steps.action: Position C-arm for AP view. Identify target level by counting from C2 (axis). Rotate to ipsilateral oblique to open the foramen.
steps.safety: Accurate level identification is critical. Count from the occiput or C2 dens as a landmark.
steps.teaching: An oblique angle of 45-60 degrees typically opens the cervical foramen. The target is the posterior aspect of the foramen to avoid the vertebral artery anteriorly.

steps.action: Select a 25-gauge, 2.5- or 3.5-inch spinal needle. Prepare contrast and non-particulate steroid (dexamethasone only).
steps.safety: ONLY non-particulate steroid (dexamethasone) should be used for cervical transforaminal injections. Particulate steroids are absolutely contraindicated.
steps.teaching: Multiple case reports document catastrophic outcomes (cerebellar and spinal cord infarction) from particulate steroids in cervical TFESI via radiculomedullary artery embolization.

steps.action: In the oblique view, advance the needle toward the posterior-superior aspect of the target foramen using an anterolateral approach.
steps.safety: The target is the posterior foramen only. Never advance into the anterior foramen where the vertebral artery lies.
steps.teaching: The posterior approach targets the space between the superior articular process posteriorly and the uncinate process anteriorly, staying posterior to the exiting nerve root.

steps.action: Check AP and lateral views to confirm needle position: tip should be at the lateral aspect of the foramen, not past the midline of the articular pillars.
steps.safety: On AP view, the needle tip should not cross the midpoint of the articular pillar. On lateral, it should remain in the posterior foramen.
steps.teaching: Multi-planar confirmation is essential for safe cervical TFESI. The lateral view distinguishes posterior from anterior foraminal position.

steps.action: Perform digital subtraction angiography (DSA) or real-time fluoroscopy during 0.3-0.5 mL contrast injection.
steps.safety: DSA is strongly recommended for cervical TFESI to detect vascular uptake. If vascular pattern is seen, reposition before injecting steroid.
steps.teaching: DSA subtracts the bony background and highlights vascular patterns that may be missed on standard fluoroscopy. A positive DSA showing arterial uptake mandates needle repositioning.

steps.action: Confirm epidural contrast pattern: nerve root sleeve outline with medial epidural spread.
steps.safety: Abort the procedure if adequate epidural spread cannot be confirmed or if the patient develops new neurological symptoms.
steps.teaching: Proper cervical epidural spread shows contrast along the nerve root and into the ventral epidural space. A periosteal pattern suggests subperiosteal placement requiring repositioning.

steps.action: Inject 0.5-1 mL dexamethasone (10 mg/mL). Total injectate volume should not exceed 1-1.5 mL.
steps.safety: Inject slowly with continuous patient communication. Stop immediately if the patient reports any new symptoms (dizziness, visual changes, weakness).
steps.teaching: Small volumes are critical in cervical TFESI to avoid compressive effects on the spinal cord. Dexamethasone 10 mg/mL provides therapeutic effect with lower risk.

steps.action: Remove needle and monitor patient for at least 30 minutes. Perform focused neurological exam before discharge.
steps.safety: Assess grip strength, upper extremity sensation, and gait before discharge. Any new deficit requires immediate evaluation.
steps.teaching: Delayed onset of neurological deficits (minutes to hours) may indicate epidural hematoma or vascular injury requiring emergent MRI and possible surgical decompression.

steps.action: Document procedure details including DSA findings, contrast pattern, injectate, fluoroscopy time, and neurological exam.
steps.safety: Document the use of non-particulate steroid and DSA to demonstrate adherence to safety standards.
steps.teaching: Documentation of safety measures (DSA, non-particulate steroid, multi-view confirmation) is essential for medicolegal protection in cervical TFESI.
